strengths: The paper poses a clear and practically relevant question—when is DPO equivalent, superior, or inferior to RLHF—and provides a well-organized dichotomy across four mis-specification regimes (none, policy-only, reward-only, double), visualized in Figure 1.

The exact-optimization analysis goes beyond the realizability assumption common in prior work, and the isomorphic-case analysis (Propositions 6-7) meaningfully extends Swamy et al. [2025] by showing online DPO can outperform both RLHF and offline DPO, while Proposition 4 shows PILAF sampling cannot close the policy mis-specification gap—a useful nuance.

The observation that the DPO policy must fit the recursively defined token-level q* function (B.10, Equation 1) whereas the RLHF reward model only needs r*, giving a structural explanation for why DPO's implicit reward model is harder to fit, is an insightful and practically relevant contribution.

The statistical separation (Theorems 10-11) is a genuinely interesting result: under sparsity, reward learning achieves O(k log d/n) error while DPO's implicit reward estimation is lower-bounded by Ω(d/n), rigorously substantiating the 'simpler ground-truth reward' hypothesis of Swamy et al. [2025].

The paper connects theory to practice twice: controlled experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF that align with each theoretical condition, plus a careful mapping of qualitative predictions onto several large-scale empirical studies (Section 5.2), which strengthens external validity.

The limitations section is honest (no algorithmic fix proposed for the BT-model reward limitation; small-scale experiments), and code is released with detailed implementation and hyper-parameter information, supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Two of the paper's dichotomy results—Proposition 4 (online DPO cannot close the policy mis-specification gap) and Proposition 7 (online DPO can outperform RLHF)—rest on 'numerical proofs' (B.8, B.9) that plot gradient curves over a bounded parameter interval rather than providing rigorous arguments. The authors themselves admit they 'didn't find elegant proofs.' For headline claims about when methods are superior, numerical evidence over a specific interval is not a substitute for a proof or at least a formal argument that the numerical solution is a genuine optimum.

The exact-optimization results in Section 3 are largely consequences of known closed-form relations (Rafailov et al., Swamy et al.) combined with small bandit constructions; Proposition 6 in particular is very close to the isomorphism result of Swamy et al. [2025]. The novelty here is mostly taxonomic (organizing conditions), which limits the technical depth of the first half.

The finite-sample separation relies on a fairly artificial construction: a dual-token task where the second token duplicates the first, a specially designed preference dataset, the constraint θ1=e1, and assumptions making the reward sparse but the DPO surrogate dense. This demonstrates possibility but leaves open how large the gap is under less engineered settings, and the sample-complexity claim is specific to this parameterization (as acknowledged).

The statistical-separation message of Section 4 overlaps with two concurrent works (Razin et al. 2026; Gopalan et al. 2026) that also show DPO is a statistically inefficient/mis-specified reward estimator; while the paper credibly differentiates approach, this reduces the distinctiveness of that contribution.

The experiments are limited to GPT-2-large on PKU-SafeRLHF with 3 seeds, and the evaluation metric (a 'score' whose definition and statistical significance are not clearly reported) is not a standard benchmark; the figures show qualitative trends rather than quantified gaps, so they corroborate but do not strongly verify the theory (e.g., no direct measurement of the second-order deviation term in Theorem 2).

The prompt space is dropped throughout the statistical analysis (Section 4 begins by 'omit[ting] prompts from now on'), and the finite-sample results are for a single fixed dataset distribution; the interaction between prompt diversity and the statistical gap is unaddressed.

Several important modeling choices are fixed without sensitivity discussion, e.g., the choice of the data-induced semi-norm as the error measure in Theorem 10, and the claim that DPO 'can only' use MLE in the lower bound deserves more care about what estimator class is permitted.

strengths: The central question—when is DPO equivalent, superior, or inferior to RLHF—is timely and practically relevant, and the decomposition of the performance gap into an explicit representation gap (exact optimization) and an implicit representation gap (finite samples) is a clean organizing principle.

Section 3 provides a reasonably complete taxonomy of misspecification regimes (reward-only, policy-only, double, isomorphic), with concrete bandit constructions demonstrating strict separations in each direction, and the observation that online DPO with sophisticated samplers (PILAF) still cannot close the policy-misspecification gap (Proposition 4) is a useful nuance.

The token-level analysis (Observation under token-level parameterization, Equation (1)) gives a plausible mechanism for why the DPO policy class faces a harder learning target than the reward model class, connecting the abstract analysis to autoregressive LMs.

The finite-sample section makes a genuine attempt at a rigorous statistical separation: the DTSP construction, together with imported sparse-recovery lemmas (Yao et al. 2025; Zhu et al. 2023), yields an upper bound O(k log d/n) for reward learning versus a lower bound Ω(d/n) for DPO's surrogate reward under sparsity, formally instantiating the 'simpler ground-truth reward' intuition of Swamy et al. (2025).

The paper is candid about limitations (no practical alternative algorithm derived from the theory, small-scale experiments) and situates its claims against concurrent work (Razin et al. 2026; Gopalan et al. 2026) and the closest prior work (Nika et al. 2024; Swamy et al. 2025).
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental relative to existing literature. The paper itself acknowledges that Swamy et al. (2025) already established the isomorphic-case equivalence and the intuition that a simpler ground-truth reward reduces sample complexity; this paper 'complements' and 'supports' those claims rather than overturning them. The Section 4 separation is also anticipated qualitatively by concurrent work (Razin et al. 2026; Gopalan et al. 2026), leaving the paper's distinctive contribution thin.

Several key propositions are not rigorously proven. Propositions 4 and 7—central claims that online DPO cannot close the policy-misspecification gap and can outperform RLHF under isomorphism—are established only by 'numerical proof' (Appendices B.8–B.9), i.e., by plotting gradients over a bounded interval and visually inspecting fixed points. For a theory paper whose headline dichotomy rests on these results, this falls short of the evidential standard; gradient-plot inspection on a bounded parameter interval does not constitute a proof of optimality or of convergence behavior.

The finite-sample separation (Theorems 10/11, formalized as 14/15) rests on heavily tailored assumptions: a specific dataset where the second token duplicates the first, a fixed known constraint θ1 = e1, a ground-truth reward engineered to be sparse plus dense, and Gram-matrix spectral conditions (Assumption 13) designed precisely so that the imported compressed-sensing lemmas apply. The Ω(d/n) vs. O(k log d/n) separation is then essentially a repackaging of known sparse-recovery bounds; its generality beyond this constructed task is asserted ('DPO could suffer...' ) rather than established.

The exact-optimization results in Section 3 are largely elementary. Propositions 1, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9 follow from definitions plus three-action bandit constructions, and Theorem 2 is a second-order Taylor expansion with a Lagrangian remainder. The qualitative upshot—'it depends on the qualities of the reward and surrogate reward models' (Figure 1)—is unsurprising, and Equation (2) reduces the entire dichotomy to a tautological statement about reward-model quality.

The experimental support is weak. All controlled experiments use GPT-2-large (774M) on a single dataset (PKU-SafeRLHF) with 3 seeds; evaluation uses the reward oracle scores, which risks circularity when the reward model itself is the object of study. The sample-efficiency experiment (Figure 4) conflates the theory's linear/sparse setting with neural network training, and the claimed agreement between the toy constructions and these runs is loose. Section 5.2's appeal to existing large-scale studies is a reasonable mitigation but is post-hoc corroboration, not independent verification.

Presentation has issues: the proliferation of Conditions 1–7 with mostly qualitative outcomes makes the main results hard to internalize; Theorems 10 and 11 are stated only informally in the main text with formal versions buried in Appendix B.11 under assumptions not visible to the main-text reader; and Figure 1 is dense and hard to parse.

The practical payoff is limited. The honest limitations section concedes that the theory does not yield a 'theoretically grounded and practically effective alternative' to the BT-model reward learning the analysis criticizes, and Appendix A's proposals (PILAF-aligned sampling, online IPO) are speculative and untested.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important and timely question—when is RLHF preferable to DPO under a representation gap—and organizes the answer into a clear and comprehensive dichotomy (no/reward/policy/double mis-specification), visualized effectively in Figure 1.

Section 3 results are supported by concrete constructions (multi-armed bandit environments with explicit feature maps) rather than only abstract claims, and the analysis of the token-level q* structure (Observation 1, Appendix B.10) gives a plausible mechanistic explanation for why the policy model faces a harder learning target than the reward model.

The statistical separation in Section 4 (Theorems 10/11) is a genuinely interesting contribution: it shows that DPO's implicit reward couples the sparse ground-truth reward with a dense soft value term, destroying sparsity, yielding a Ω(d/n) lower bound versus O(k log d/n) for explicit reward learning. This formalizes and extends intuitions from Yao et al. (2025) and Swamy et al. (2025) in a meaningful way.

Experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF are carefully designed to isolate each theoretical condition, and the paper thoughtfully connects its qualitative predictions to multiple independent large-scale empirical studies (Section 5.2), which strengthens external validity given the intentionally small-scale controlled experiments.

The limitations discussion is honest and specific (no principled fix for BT-model reward learning under mis-specification; small-scale experiments), and implementation details, hyperparameters, and released code support reproducibility.

The treatment of online DPO (Proposition 4, Theorem 2) is a useful nuance: even sophisticated samplers like PILAF cannot close the policy mis-specification gap, which prior work had not clearly established.
weaknesses: Two of the Section 3 claims (Propositions 4 and 7) are established only by 'numerical proof'—plotting gradient curves on a one-parameter family—rather than rigorous argument (Appendices B.8–B.9). The authors candidly admit they 'didn't find elegant proofs,' but for a main-track theory paper these central dichotomy results deserve formal proofs; as stated, these propositions are only conjectures supported by simulation.

A substantial portion of the Section 3 results are close relatives of known results: the isomorphic equivalence (Proposition 6) essentially restates Swamy et al. (2025), the upper-bound decomposition in B.12 is standard performance-difference-lemma bookkeeping, and Theorem 2 is a direct Taylor-expansion comparison of objectives analogous to Feng et al. (2025). The genuinely new content is concentrated in the sparse-reward separation of Section 4, which itself leans heavily on lemmas imported from Yao et al. (2025).

The lower bound for DPO (Ω(d/n)) holds for a specific DTSP construction in which the DPO target parameter is necessarily dense; the paper does not explore whether DPO-side estimators with structural priors (e.g., regularization reflecting the r_sparse + r_dense decomposition) could partially close the gap. The separation is therefore somewhat tailored to the chosen estimators, and the 'informal' framing of Theorem 11 vs. the formal Theorem 14 makes the headline claims harder to assess at a glance.

The exact-optimization analysis omits prompts ('we can simply sum over different prompts') and assumes a contextless bandit; several constructions use degenerate feature configurations (e.g., a known θ₁ = e₁ constraint, one-hot features, hand-set β = 0.1 or θ-projections with threshold 20), so the practical prevalence of each mis-specification regime is argued more by plausibility (e.g., 6B vs. 175B parameter asymmetry) than by measurement.

Experiments are small-scale (GPT-2-large, one dataset, 3 seeds) and some evidence is indirect: Figure 2's support for Theorem 2 rests on a second-order deviation effect, and Figure 4 measures reward-model accuracy rather than downstream policy sub-optimality, which is the actual quantity in Theorem 11. Hyperparameters are admittedly not extensively tuned, raising the possibility that some gaps reflect optimization artifacts rather than the theory.

There is significant overlap with concurrent work (Razin et al. 2026; Gopalan et al. 2026) on DPO as a mis-specified reward estimator; while the paper distinguishes its approach, the marginal novelty over this concurrent line is reduced and should be more precisely delineated.

strengths: The paper provides a clear, well-organized taxonomy of the RLHF-vs-DPO performance gap, decomposing it into a representation gap (exact optimization under four mis-specification regimes) and a statistical gap (finite-sample reward learning), summarized accessibly in Table 1.

The mis-specification analysis is backed by concrete, explicit constructions (multi-armed bandit examples in Appendices C.3–C.9) establishing that each direction of the gap is achievable, including the notable result that online DPO with the PILAF sampler cannot close the policy-mis-specification gap (Proposition 4), which the authors correctly identify as an overlooked phenomenon.

The statistical separation result (Theorems 10/11/14/15) is a genuine technical contribution: it extends sparse reward recovery results (Yao et al., 2025) to a dual-token token-level linear setting and proves a lower bound of Ω(d/n) for any DPO estimator, giving a clean ℓ0/ℓ1 vs. Θ(d/n) separation. Proofs appear careful and adapt compressed-sensing techniques properly.

The paper situates itself honestly relative to prior work, particularly Nika et al. (2024) and Swamy et al. (2026), clearly articulating what is new (regularized metric, mis-specification analysis under exact optimization, sparsity-based statistical separation), and discusses concurrent works.

Controlled experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF with GPT-2 corroborate each theoretical regime qualitatively, and the paper connects its predictions to multiple existing large-scale empirical studies, increasing practical relevance. Code and implementation details are provided, supporting reproducibility.
Limitations are candidly discussed (no practical alternative algorithm offered, small-scale experiments, two-token restriction for the statistical result).
weaknesses: Substantial overlap with prior work reduces originality: the isomorphic-case analysis extends the hypothesis of Swamy et al. (2026); the linear-reward statistical bounds build directly on Nika et al. (2024); the sparse-recovery machinery is imported from Yao et al. (2025); Theorem 2 is acknowledged as analogous to Feng et al. (2025). The main novelty is consolidation, concretization, and the DPO lower bound in the dual-token setting.

Several constructions rely on degenerate or unnatural model classes (e.g., Construction 2 of Proposition 8 defines the reward class F as a singleton {θ_R}; some constructions use artificially constrained policy classes such as a half-space constraint on θ), which weakens the practical interpretability of the 'either method can win' claims.

The experiments are quite small-scale (GPT-2-large, ~10k samples, safety dataset only), hyperparameters are admittedly not extensively tuned, and the exact-optimization verification plots (Figures 1–2) show only 2–3 'iterations' with qualitative trends; they corroborate but do not strongly test the theory.

The statistical separation holds only for a two-token task under sparsity of the ground-truth reward and strong Gram-matrix/spectral assumptions; the authors concede the intuition does not formally extend to multi-token sequences, limiting the reach of the headline sample-complexity claim. The ℓ0-constrained estimator is also computationally intractable, so the strongest separation bound is oracle-based.

The approximate-optimization analysis assumes the data distribution asymptotically equals the on-policy distribution (justified only heuristically), and the connection between the reward-quality framework (Equation 2) and the concrete sparse construction is loose—arguably two somewhat disjoint papers stitched together.

Presentation has minor rough edges: informal theorem statements in the main text with formal versions only in the appendix, occasional numbering/typographical issues (e.g., 'Lemmas'), and Remark 7's admission that the lower-bound proof requires a specific vocabulary construction where prior work (Nika et al., 2024) already covers the general case.

strengths: The paper offers a systematic, well-organized taxonomy of the RLHF vs. DPO performance gap, decomposing it into explicit representation gap (seven misspecification conditions, Conditions 1–7) and implicit representation gap from finite-sample estimation, which gives practitioners a usable map of when each method should be preferred.

Several results contain genuinely non-obvious insights: Proposition 4 shows that even online DPO with the PILAF sampler cannot close the gap under policy model mis-specification, and Theorem 2 quantifies a second-order deviation term of the online DPO objective that grows with reward scale — an effect later visualized experimentally (Figure 1, reward scale 0.4/1/4).

The statistical separation (Theorems 10/11) is a concrete construction showing DPO's surrogate parameter θ_p is inherently dense while the ground-truth reward parameter can be sparse, yielding Ω(d/n) vs. Ũ(k log d/n) errors; the authors connect the sparsity assumption to empirical measurements (Yao et al., 2025), which partially mitigates concerns about artificiality.

The controlled experiments are deliberately designed to isolate each theoretical condition, and the authors additionally map their qualitative predictions onto multiple independent large-scale empirical studies (Section 5.2), which strengthens external validity beyond the small GPT-2 setup.

Reproducibility is adequate: code is released, datasets and hyper-parameters are documented, experiments are run over 3 seeds, and the limitations (two-token analysis, small-scale models, lack of a theoretically grounded alternative reward-learning objective) are honestly acknowledged rather than hidden.

The appendix is thorough: formal statements, full proofs for all propositions, and derivations of the 'real' reward objective (Appendix B) that yield an interpretable ℓ2 pairwise-difference characterization and a principled motivation for the PILAF sampler.
weaknesses: The core statistical separation rests on restrictive and somewhat oracle-like machinery: the ℓ0-constrained reward estimator is given the support of r_sparse (the constraint set θ0 + e1 + r_sparse + {‖θ‖0 ≤ k, θ_{e1}=e1} presupposes knowledge of the sparse support and the dense direction), and the setup is limited to a two-token DTSP task with well-conditioned Gram-matrix assumptions. The authors admit the sparsity/singularity properties do not extend to three or more tokens, so the headline sample-complexity dichotomy is established only in a specialized regime.

A substantial fraction of the exact-optimization results is conceptually expected or follows known observations: Proposition 1 is immediate; the policy/reward misspecification directions were already articulated by Swamy et al. (2026) and Nika et al. (2024), and the authors themselves frame their work as 'extending' the isomorphism hypothesis of Swamy et al. (2026). Novelty is thus incremental and partly overlapping with concurrent works (Razin et al., 2026a/b; Gopalan et al., 2026; Ackermann et al., 2025), which limits the contribution's distinctiveness.

Several 'theorems' are established by small hand-crafted bandit constructions (3-action bandits with 2-dimensional features, and in one case a solution verified only 'numerically' over x(θ) ∈ [−4, 4] before a tedious formal derivation). While such counterexamples are legitimate for showing impossibility, they provide little quantitative insight into how large the gap is in realistic settings.

The experimental verification is small-scale (GPT-2-Large on PKU-SafeRLHF, 9k preference pairs), the RLHF baseline uses a pairwise regression surrogate rather than PPO, and hyper-parameters were admittedly not extensively tuned; some plots (e.g., Figure 2, Condition 4) are interpreted post hoc through the relative expressiveness of F versus F_Π rather than predicted a priori.

The main text states theorems informally and defers all formal statements to the appendix; combined with the heavy condition taxonomy, a reader must hold many definitions in mind before the central claims become precise, which weakens the accessibility of the contribution.

The bonus section (Appendix B) proposes aligning MLE with the 'real' objective via a Taylor step and PILAF-style sampling, but provides no theory or experiments for this modification, leaving the practical remedy underdeveloped despite the paper's own acknowledgment that it 'could be beneficial … but still limited'.

strengths: The paper provides a clean, well-organized decomposition of the RLHF–DPO performance gap into exact-optimization (representation/mis-specification) and approximate-optimization (statistical efficiency) sources, summarized usefully in Table 1.

The mis-specification analysis in Section 3 is systematic: it covers all realizability combinations and, importantly, the double mis-specification regime with isomorphic model classes, where concrete constructions (Propositions 3–9) establish strict separations in both directions, including the novel and non-obvious observation that even PILAF-style online sampling cannot close the gap under policy mis-specification (Proposition 4).

The statistical separation in Section 4 (Theorems 10/11, formally 14/15) is a genuine contribution: a lower bound of Ω(d/n) for the DPO surrogate parameter under token-level linear parameterization with sparse rewards, versus O(k log d/n) and Õ(√(k log d/n)) for ℓ0/ℓ1-constrained reward estimators, with proofs that adapt compressed-sensing-style arguments (relative-constrained estimators) to the preference-learning setting.

The controlled experiments on PKU-SafeRLHF are designed to directly test each theoretical regime, and Section 5.2 thoughtfully connects the theory to existing large-scale empirical observations (Razin et al., Xu et al., Ivison et al.), strengthening external validity.

Concurrent and closely related works (Nika et al. 2024; Swamy et al. 2026; Razin et al. 2026; Gopalan et al. 2026; Ackermann et al. 2025) are discussed honestly and the deltas over them are articulated clearly, including a different performance metric and stronger statistical separation (Θ(d/n) vs Θ(√(d_R/n)) with d_P = d_R).

Limitations are acknowledged candidly (no practical alternative algorithm proposed, small-scale experiments, multi-token cases deferred), and implementation details, code release, and hyper-parameters support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The exact-optimization results (Propositions 1–9) are largely built from small multi-armed bandit constructions with 2–3 actions; while clean and correct, they are relatively straightforward counterexamples, and the qualitative takeaways partially echo what concurrent work (Swamy et al. 2026) already hypothesized or proved, reducing the novelty of Section 3 on its own.

The statistical separation relies on quite restrictive assumptions: token-level linear parameterization, two-token responses with the second token duplicating the first, a known anchor (θ^*_0 = e_1) so that the relative-constrained estimator is well-defined, well-conditioned Gram matrices, and — most notably — an ℓ0-constrained estimator that is computationally intractable; the achievable gap for the practical ℓ1 estimator is smaller, and the authors themselves note the results do not extend directly to three or more tokens.

The experimental verification is very small scale (GPT-2-Large, ~5k–10k samples, 3 seeds, 3–4 iterations per run), the 'score' metric plotted in Figures 1–3 is not precisely defined in the main text, and y-axis ranges are small (e.g., roughly -0.1 to 0.2), making it hard to judge statistical significance or practical magnitude of the gaps; hyper-parameters were not extensively tuned.

Several headline theorems appear only in informal form in the main text, with the burden of verifying assumptions (e.g., Assumptions 12–13, feature-mapping constructions) pushed to the appendix; a reader cannot fully assess applicability without this extra work.

The practical guidance, while sensible ('learn an explicit reward model when rewards are sparse/simple; the policy target is intrinsically richer'), remains qualitative: the paper does not provide an algorithmic remedy or a theory-guided estimator that practitioners could deploy, and the Appendix B discussion of improved objectives is left as future work.

Some intermediate regimes (partially overlapping model classes) are explicitly excluded 'for the sake of a principled analysis', which slightly weakens the claimed comprehensiveness of the 'dichotomy'.
